procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 6, 1967 of the Kerala High Court in Criminal Appeals Nos. 114 to 124 of 1967.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Kerala High Court heard Criminal Appeals Nos. 114 to 124 of 1967 and issued a judgment and order on September 6, 1967. The High Court's decision was in favor of the respondent.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the High Court's judgment and order to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court heard Criminal Appeals Nos. 145 to 156 of 1968.

issue.issue_text: Whether the exemption under Section 16(1)(b) of the Employees' Provident Funds Act, 1952 is available for the first three years from the date the Act became applicable to an establishment, or from the date the establishment was first set up.

facts: The High Court had acquitted the respondent on the legal ground that under Section 16(1)(b) of the Act, an establishment is exempt for a period of 3 years from the date on which the Act became applicable to it (in this case, 1961).
law: The Supreme Court relied on its previous decision in *R. Ramakrishna Rao v. State of Kerala*.
This precedent held that the exemption period under Section 16(1)(b) is counted forward from the date the establishment is "set up".
application: Applying the precedent, the Court reasoned that if the establishment was the original one set up in 1946, the exemption period would run from that date.
The exemption could not be counted from April 1961, which was merely the date the Act became applicable to the establishment (due to an increase in the number of employees).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning and held that the exemption under Section 16(1)(b) is available for the first three years from the date the establishment was first set up, not from the date the Act became applicable to it.

issue.issue_text: Whether, on the facts of the case, the establishment purchased by the respondent society in 1961 was a continuation of the old establishment set up in 1946, or an entirely new establishment.

facts: A new owner, the N.S.S. Co-operative Society, purchased the establishment in 1961.
After the purchase, there was a break in operations for about three months.
The machinery in the Press was altered, and additional machinery was purchased.
The previous employees were not continued in service; instead, the previous owner paid them compensation, indicating their services were terminated.
The new owner conducted a fresh recruitment of employees, and only six of the new hires happened to be previous employees (who were described as "re-employed").
The establishment was not purchased as a "going concern."
law: The burden of proving that the old establishment had continued and was not a new one rested on the appellant (the prosecution).
application: The Supreme Court examined the evidence and found that the appellant failed to meet the burden of proof required to show continuity.

The Court determined that the combination of facts—a new owner, a three-month closure, altered machinery, and a complete change in the workforce (evidenced by the termination, compensation payments, and fresh recruitment)—demonstrated a clear lack of continuity.
The payment of compensation to the old workers was seen as significant evidence that their employment had ended with the previous owner.
The Court concluded that these facts overwhelmingly supported the respondent's argument that the old business was completely closed and a new one was started.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that, based on the facts, the establishment purchased by the respondent society in 1961 was not a continuation of the old one. Instead, the old establishment was completely closed, and an entirely new establishment was set up three months after the purchase.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the exemption under Section 16(1)(b) of the Employees' Provident Funds Act, 1952 is available for the first three years from the date the Act became applicable to an establishment, or from the date the establishment was first set up.
appellant_arguments: The exemption period under Section 16(1)(b) runs from the date on which the establishment was first set up, not from the date the Act became applicable to it.
respondent_arguments: The exemption period should be counted from the date the Act became applicable to the establishment (April 1961).

arguments.issue_text: Whether, on the facts of the case, the establishment purchased by the respondent society in 1961 was a continuation of the old establishment set up in 1946, or an entirely new establishment.
appellant_arguments: The establishment was a continuation of the old one set up in 1946. (This is inferred as the text states 'The burden of proving that the old establishment had continued was on the appellant.')
respondent_arguments: The old establishment ceased to exist and an entirely new one was set up in 1961.
The society did not purchase the establishment as a going concern.
There was a closure for about 3 months after the purchase, and a new business was started.
The workmen of the previous owner were not taken over on their old conditions of service; they were paid termination compensation.
Fresh appointments were made and all workers were newly recruited, even if some were former employees.
The sale-deed specifically provided that none of the old workers were to be taken into service.

cases.principle: The exemption period under s. 16(1)(b) is counted from the date an establishment is set up, not from the date the Act becomes applicable to it.

cases.case_name: Virtaldas Jagannathadas & Anr. v. Regional Provident Fund Commissioner & Anr.
cases.principle: The exemption under s. 16(1)(b) of the Act is available from the date an establishment was set up, not from the date the Act became applicable to it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Upon a transfer of ownership, an old establishment is considered completely closed and a new establishment is set up when there is a significant break in operations, alteration of machinery, non-continuation of the previous workforce with fresh recruitment, and payment of terminal compensation to the former employees by the previous owner.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Although the High Court's legal interpretation of Section 16(1)(b) was incorrect, the respondent's acquittal is upheld on factual grounds. After reviewing the evidence, the Court found that the establishment purchased by the respondent society in 1961 was not a continuation of the old one, but an entirely new establishment. Therefore, it was entitled to a fresh three-year exemption period starting from 1961, which covered the period of the alleged offenses.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the precedent from R. Ramakrishna Rao v. State of Kerala, which established that under Section 16(1)(b), the exemption period for a new establishment is counted forward from the date it is set up, but for an existing establishment, it is counted from the date the establishment 'had been' set up.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant lost the appeal because the Court, after reviewing the trial evidence, overturned the High Court's factual finding and concluded that the respondent had successfully proven that the establishment was entirely new and not a continuation of the one set up in 1946.

While the appellant correctly argued the point of law regarding the start date of the exemption period for an existing establishment, this legal victory was rendered moot by the Court's factual determination that this was a new establishment.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that, on the facts, the old establishment ceased to exist and an entirely new one was set up in 1961. The Court, after being taken through the evidence, stated, 'we are inclined to accept the submission made on behalf of the respondent.'

Because the Court found that a new establishment was set up in 1961, the provisions of Section 16(1)(b) granted it a three-year exemption from that date, absolving it of any liability for the period to which the prosecutions related.
policy_considerations: The provided text does not contain any explicit policy considerations from the Supreme Court. It notes the High Court's view that the exemption is for 'treating the establishment as an infant establishment standing in need of protection,' but the Supreme Court's own reasoning is based strictly on precedent and a factual analysis of the evidence.
